column2: Those who are wealthy, brave, skilled in arms and masters of the scriptures bring republics safely through hard calamities when they are bewildered.
Anger, division, fear, the rod, harassment, restraint and killing quickly bring republics under the enemy's power, best of the Bharatas.
Therefore those chiefs of the republic must be honoured above all; the great business of the world depends upon them, king.
Secrecy of counsel rests with the leaders, and spies too, scourge of foes; republics as a whole are not fit to hear counsel, Bharata.
The republic's welfare should be done together with its chiefs, among themselves; otherwise, with the republic divided and at odds, aims come to ruin and misfortunes arise.
The wise should quickly restrain, chiefly through their leaders, those who, divided from one another, follow their own power.
Quarrels born in families, neglected by the elders of the families, bring about, king, a splitting of the republic through the clan.
Fear from within must be guarded, fear from without is easily guarded; fear born within cuts away the root at once.
Suddenly, from anger or greed or even delusion, born of nature, if they do not speak to one another—that is the mark of their defeat.
All are alike in birth and alike in family, but not in valour, in intellect, or again in beauty and wealth.
Through division and carelessness republics are bowed down by enemies; therefore they say that union is the great refuge of republics."
Which duty, in your opinion, is weightier than all the dharmas, so that this man may gain dharma here and hereafter?
[Bhishma said:] "Worship of mother and father and teachers is highly esteemed by me; a man engaged in this wins worlds and great fame.
Whatever deed these, well honoured, know to be right, dear one, whether in accord with dharma or against it, that should be done, Yudhishthira.
One should not devise any other dharma without their leave; whatever these approve is dharma—that is certain.
These alone are the three worlds, these alone the three stages of life, these alone the three Vedas, these alone the three fires.
The father is the Garhapatya fire, the mother is called the Dakshina fire, the teacher is the Ahavaniya; the triad of fires is weightier.
Not neglecting these three, you will conquer the three worlds: by serving the father this world, by serving the mother the other, and by the teacher's service you will ever move in Brahma's world.
Behave rightly toward these three in the three worlds, Bharata; you will gain fame, good fortune, and dharma of great fruit.
Neither this world nor the other is his, scorcher of foes, for whom these three elders are ever dishonoured.
Neither in this world nor the next does his fame shine, nor is any other good of the hereafter declared for him.
From them alone I release all that, by service; it was a hundredfold and a thousandfold for me; therefore the three worlds shine for me, Yudhishthira.
One good teacher surpasses ten Shrotriyas; an upadhyaya ten teachers; a father ten upadhyayas.
The mother alone surpasses ten fathers, or even the whole earth, in greatness; there is no teacher like a mother. The mother is a greater teacher than the father—so I hold.
Both mother and father serve at birth; these two make the body, father and mother, Bharata; but the birth that the teacher instructs is divine, ageless and deathless.
The mother and father are always not to be slain, even when they do wrong; he is not corrupted by doing that, nor do they corrupt him; the gods with the sages know this of those striving for dharma.
He who fills the ears with unfailing truth, speaking the true and giving the immortal—him I deem father and mother; one should not injure him, knowing what he has done.
Those who, having heard knowledge, do not respect the teacher who is near, in mind or act—as they are to be honoured by their teachers, so their teachers too are to be honoured.
Therefore teachers should be worshipped and shared with, with effort, and honoured, by one who wishes the ancient dharma.
By whatever pleases the fathers, the grandfather is pleased; by whatever pleases the mother, the earth is honoured.
By whatever pleases the teacher, Brahman is honoured; the teacher is thus more to be honoured than mother or father; and the sages are pleased with the gods and the ancestors.
In no conduct should the teacher be despised; neither mother nor father is like the teacher.
They deserve no insult, nor do they corrupt him; the gods with the sages know honour of the teachers alone.
Those who injure their upadhyaya, father or mother in mind or deed, their sin is worse than the killing of an embryo; there is no sinner other than they in the world.
For the betrayer of a friend, the ungrateful, the slayer of a woman and the slanderer, we have not heard of an atonement for these four.
All this has been set forth in brief, what a man should do in this world; this is the highest good, nothing else is better than this; it has been said following all the dharmas."

Truth and falsehood both stand pervading the worlds; of these, which should a man firm in dharma practise, king?
mahabharata:12:110.3	What is truth, what falsehood, what is the eternal dharma? At what time should he speak truth, and at what time falsehood?
[Bhishma said:] "Speaking truth is good; there is nothing higher than truth; what is very hard to know on earth, that I shall tell you, Bharata.
Sometimes truth should not be spoken and falsehood should be spoken; where falsehood would be truth, or truth would be falsehood.
In such a case the childish are bewildered, where truth is not settled; having ascertained truth and falsehood, one then becomes a knower of dharma.
Even an ignoble man, of untrained understanding, quite cruel, may gain very great merit, like Balaka from killing the blind one.
What wonder that a fool, desiring dharma yet ignorant of it, may gain very great sin, like Kaushika at the Ganga?
Such is this question, in which dharma is very hard to state, difficult to determine, and is settled here by reasoning.
If release is possible by not crying out, one should not cry out at all; or if one must cry out, or they would suspect from silence...
In such a case it is better to speak falsehood than truth, so it is held: one who is freed from association with sinners by an oath.
Nor should wealth be given to them in any way when it is possible not to; wealth given to sinners would torment even the giver.
Those witnesses who, wishing to take a boon at the cost of their own bodies, say anything anywhere to gain assent to truth without saying what ought to be said there—all are speakers of falsehood.
When life is at stake and at a marriage, falsehood may be spoken, to protect wealth, or for the dharma of others; one who desires the dharma of others would be a base beggar of dharma.
What has been promised should be given, but tomorrow it is to be done under compulsion; whoever has fallen from the agreement of dharma and stands in adharma,
the rogue who gives up his own dharma and wishes to live by it, the sinner who lives by fraud, is to be slain by all means.
Wealth is the settled aim of all sinners here; those who are unbearable, not to dine with, fallen by fraud,
fallen from gods and men, are like the dead; separation from life is more painful than taking their wealth.
May this dharma please you—it should be said with effort; but there is no dharma for sinners—this is certain.
One who slays such a person is not stained by sin; he slays one slain by his own deed, and the slain is slain indeed. Whoever makes an agreement with those of ruined mind...
Like the crow and the vulture are those who live by deceit; after release from the body they are born in such wombs.
As a man behaves toward one, so should one behave toward him—that is dharma; one of deceitful conduct is to be dealt with by deceit; one of good conduct is to be met with good."
[Bhishma said:] "Twice-born who, restrained in self, live as prescribed in the stages as prescribed, cross over difficulties.
Those who do not mutter from hypocrisy, whose livelihood is concealed and who restrain the objects of sense, cross over difficulties.
Those who always lodge guests and are free from envy, always given to study, cross over difficulties.
Those who, knowing dharma, behave dutifully toward mother and father and avoid sleep by day, cross over difficulties.
Those who, in the proper season each time, go to their own wives in lawful conduct and are devoted to the agnihotra, being good, cross over difficulties.
Kings, clouded by passion, who do not take wealth out of greed, and guard their lands, cross over difficulties.
Those who are heroes in battles, giving up fear of death and desiring victory by dharma, cross over difficulties.
Those who do no sins by deed, mind or speech, and lay down the rod toward beings, cross over difficulties.
Brahmanas who do not neglect study on non-study days, ever devoted to austerity and of fine austerity, cross over difficulties.
Those whose deeds are not for show, whose speech is truthful and kind, and whose wealth is for good ends, cross over difficulties.
Those who practise austerity, celibate from youth, bathed in knowledge and Vedic vows, cross over difficulties.
Those whose passion is stilled and whose darkness is stilled, great souls established in truth, cross over difficulties.
Those of whom no one is afraid and who are afraid of no one, for whom the world is like themselves, cross over difficulties.
The good, bulls among men, who are not pained by another's prosperity and who have turned from village food, cross over difficulties.
Those who bow to all the gods, hear all the dharmas, and have faith and self-control, cross over difficulties.
Those who do not desire honour but honour others, and when honoured do not think themselves so, cross over difficulties.
Those who, desiring offspring, perform shraddhas on each lunar day with a very pure mind, cross over difficulties.
Those who never become angry, who calm the angry, and are not angry at servants, cross over difficulties.
Men who here always avoid honey, meat and, from birth, strong drink, cross over difficulties.
Those whose eating is for the journey of life, whose union is for offspring, and whose speech is for the speaking of truth, cross over difficulties.
Devotees of Narayana, lord of all beings, the origin and dissolution of the world, cross over difficulties.
This red-lotus-eyed, yellow-robed, mighty-armed Achyuta is your friend, brother, companion and relative.
He, lord of inconceivable self, Govinda, the Supreme Person, who could wrap all these worlds like a skin if he wished,
stands in the pleasure and welfare of Jishnu, bull among men; and for you too, king, the unassailable Vaikuntha, Supreme Person.
Those who here take refuge in Narayana Hari with devotion cross over difficulties here; I have no doubt of this.
Those who read this passage on crossing difficulties, make others hear it, and have it recited to Brahmanas, cross over difficulties.
Thus the summary of duty has been recounted to you by me, sinless one, by which a man may cross difficulties hereafter and here."
[Bhishma said:] "On this too they recite this ancient history, the conversation of a tiger and a jackal; hear it, Yudhishthira.
Long ago in the city of Purika, the fortunate, there was a king of the city, a cruel man, fond of harming others, the lowest of men.
When his life was exhausted he went to an undesired state, and became a jackal, stained by his former deeds.
Remembering his former birth, he reached the utmost disgust; he would not eat flesh even when brought by others.
Harmless to all beings, truthful and firm in his vows, he made his food, as he liked, of fallen fruits.
The jackal's dwelling came to be in the cremation ground, by his preference; and out of regard for his birthplace he liked no other dwelling.
Unable to bear his purity, all his fellow jackals sought to shake that resolve with deferential words:
Living in the dread ancestors' grove, you wish to attain purity? This contradiction is yours, since you are a flesh-eater.

If my dwelling is in the cremation ground, hear my meditation: the self bears fruit by its deeds; the stage of life is not the mark of dharma.
mahabharata:12:112.14	If a man in a hermitage should kill a Brahmana, or one outside a hermitage should give a cow, would that not be sin, or would that gift not be in vain?
mahabharata:12:112.15	You, out of every greed, delight only in eating; deluded, you do not see the faults that follow after.
mahabharata:12:112.16	A livelihood made of distrust, blameworthy, spoiled by wrong-doing in wealth, bad here and hereafter—therefore I do not like it.
Thinking him pure and wise, a tiger of famed prowess, honouring him as his equal, himself advanced him to be his counsellor:

Gentle one, with your nature known, come with me on the journey; let the enjoyments you desire be chosen, and ample things be kept away.
mahabharata:12:112.19	We are known as fierce, and we make it known to you; those who strike first mildly will find good fortune.
Then, honouring the words of that great lord of beasts, the jackal, bowing a little, spoke respectful words:

This speech of yours, king of beasts, is fitting in me, that you seek helpers skilled in dharma and wealth and pure.
mahabharata:12:112.22	One cannot rule greatness without ministers, or with evil ministers, hero, who obstruct one's welfare.
mahabharata:12:112.23	One should seek helpers who are devoted, not covetous, not quarrelling with one another, wishing to win, not greedy,
mahabharata:12:112.24	free of deceit, wise, intent on welfare, high-minded, great and fortunate—you should honour them as teachers, as fathers.
mahabharata:12:112.25	But for my contentment I like nothing else, lord of beasts; I do not desire pleasures and enjoyments or lordship dependent on you.
mahabharata:12:112.26	My nature will not fit with your old servants; they will be divided from you, being of painful temper, because of me.
mahabharata:12:112.27	You are a refuge to be praised, even for other brilliant ones; self-perfected, greatly fortunate, not cruel even to sinners,
mahabharata:12:112.28	far-sighted, of great energy, openhanded, of great strength, accomplished, unerring in deed and adorned with what is to be—
mahabharata:12:112.29	but I am content with my own; a hard livelihood is practised; and I do not know service, a free forest-ranger.
mahabharata:12:112.30	All the faults of the king's neighbourhood belong to those who dwell in dependence; the forest life is unattached, fearless and unconfined.
mahabharata:12:112.31	The fear that sits in the heart of one summoned by a king does not sit in the contented who eat roots and fruits in the forest.
mahabharata:12:112.32	Water without exertion or sweet food mixed with fear—weighing it, I see that as happiness in which there is peace.
mahabharata:12:112.33	Servants are not so punished by kings for offences as they are ruined by plots and brought to destruction.
mahabharata:12:112.34	But if this is to be done by me, and the lord of beasts agrees, I wish a covenant to be kept regarding me:
mahabharata:12:112.35	Those of mine should be honoured by you; my good counsel should be heard; and the livelihood that has been arranged for you should be firmly kept.
I would never take counsel with your other ministers; seeking advantage, the clever would speak idly to me.
One by one, meeting you in private, I shall tell you what is good; and in the affairs of your kin I am not to be asked about good or ill.
After consulting me, the ministers should not be harmed by you; and angry, do not let the rod fall on those of mine."
So be it, said the lord of beasts, honouring him; and the jackal, from a tiger's birth, obtained the post of minister by his wisdom.
Seeing him so honoured and employed in work, the former servants, banded together, hated him again and again.
With friendly mind they comforted the jackal and brought him in, and the ill-minded wished to bring him to equality in faults.
For otherwise, being accustomed to seizing others' goods, unable to take anything, they were checked by the jackal.
Wishing his fall, they tempted him with stories, and his mind was tempted with great wealth.
But that greatly wise one did not waver from his steadiness; then, having made an agreement, the others stood for his destruction.
The meat that was prepared there, desired by the lord of beasts, they themselves removed and placed in his dwelling.
He knew all that—why it was taken, by whom, and what was counselled—and for a reason he endured it.
This agreement was made by him on becoming minister: You should not take harm to me, king, if you wish friendship here."
When the meal was to be brought, that meat was not to be seen; and the king of beasts ordered, "Let the thief be sought."
With artifice they described that meat to the lord of beasts: "It was brought by your minister, wise in his own conceit."
Hearing the jackal's fickleness, the tiger was angry; the king was offended and approved his slaying.
Seeing that gap, the former ministers said: "He is bent on breaking the livelihood of us all.
And this deed of his is guarded by favour; and as heard before by the master, he is not as he seems.
He is righteous in speech alone but cruel by nature; this sinner is a mask of dharma, taking pains in vain conduct, in vows for the sake of work and food."
Knowing that the meat had been taken, the tiger, hearing their words, then commanded: "Let the jackal be killed."
Hearing the tiger's words, the tiger's mother came to enlighten the lord of beasts with good words:

Son, you should not accept this, cloaked in a beginning of deceit; the pure is corrupted by impure faults born of the friction of deeds.
mahabharata:12:112.57	No one tolerates one who has risen; the work of enmity is done; even for a pure man, intent, only a fault is cast down.
mahabharata:12:112.58	The pure are hated by the greedy, the strong by cowards, the learned by fools, the wealthy by the poor, the righteous by the unrighteous, the handsome by the ugly.
mahabharata:12:112.59	Many learned men are greedy and all live by deceit; they might fault even a blameless man of Brihaspati's wisdom.
mahabharata:12:112.60	The meat taken today from the empty house—he does not wish it even when given; let that be well considered first.
mahabharata:12:112.61	By fate, things are seen as untrue that look true, and true that look untrue; in them examination is proper.
mahabharata:12:112.62	The sky seems to have a floor, and the firefly seems like a fire; yet there is no floor in the sky nor fire in the firefly.
mahabharata:12:112.63	Therefore even what is seen directly it is proper to examine; he who, having examined, makes known matters does not afterwards repent.
mahabharata:12:112.64	It is not hard, son, for a lord to have another killed; but forbearance of the powerful is praised and chosen in the world.
mahabharata:12:112.65	This one, renowned among the neighbouring chiefs, was set up by you, son; a worthy vessel is hard to find; keep this friend.
mahabharata:12:112.66	Whoever takes the pure otherwise, corrupted by others' faults, himself corrupting his ministers, soon perishes.
Then someone came from the enemy band of the jackal, a righteous-souled man, and told how this deceit had been done.
Then, his conduct known, he was honoured and released, and embraced with affection again and again by the lord of beasts.
But the jackal, versed in the science of policy, took leave of the lord of beasts, and, burning with that indignation, wished to fast to death.
The tiger, tears flowing from affection, restrained the righteous jackal, returning honour with honour.
The jackal, seeing him come in haste from affection, bowing, spoke with a voice choked with tears:

I was honoured by you before and then dishonoured; I was taken to the haunt of others; I cannot live with you.
mahabharata:12:112.73	Servants who were content with their own, who fell from place and were lowered from honour, or who were taken and brought by others themselves,
mahabharata:12:112.74	the exhausted, the greedy, the cruel, the tormented in prison, the proud who have lost their goods, and the ambitious who have been abandoned or taken up,
mahabharata:12:112.75	those who are tormented, who watch for calamity, hidden, supported—all of these are tools.
mahabharata:12:112.76	How will you go to trust me, set up again though joined with insult, or shall I come again?
mahabharata:12:112.77	Having taken me as capable, set me up, tested me, and having broken the agreement made, you have dishonoured me.
mahabharata:12:112.78	One first declared in the assembly to be of good character—his defects should not be spoken of, by one guarding his promise.
mahabharata:12:112.79	Thus, dishonoured here, what trust will you give me? And in your want of trust, my own anxiety will arise.
mahabharata:12:112.80	You are suspicious, I am afraid, the enemies watch for gaps, the unaffectionate are hard to satisfy, and this business is much deceit.
mahabharata:12:112.81	What is broken is joined with difficulty, and what is joined is broken with difficulty; the love that is broken and joined does not proceed with affection.
mahabharata:12:112.82	Someone is seen to be afraid, but not of another and himself; feelings depend on regard to purpose; the affectionate are rare.

Having thus spoken with many kinds of conciliation, with reasons of dharma and wealth, and having appeased the king, the jackal went to the forest.
Not accepting the lord of beasts' entreaty, the wise jackal, sitting in fast to death, gave up his body and went to heaven."
[Bhishma said:] "Now I shall tell you; hear the one settled course of duty—what a king should do here, and by doing which he would be happy.
One should not behave as we have heard of the great conduct of the camel; hear that, Yudhishthira.
A great camel who remembered his former births, born in the age of Prajapati, practised very great austerity in the forest, firm in his vows.
At the end of his austerity the lord was pleased, and then the grandfather offered him a boon.
So it is not I, nor Death, nor the serpent, nor you, nor this old Brahmana woman; the child alone is the cause here.
But when that king of the city reached the utmost distress, he blew his horn, and then a force appeared.
And especially I burn, for fifteen years now; I am bound, ill-minded, for the purification of this sin.
Hearing that, Satyabhama wept and went to Keshava's side, enraged and angering Janardana.
[Yudhishthira said:] "O lord of the past and future, this dog is ever devoted to me; let him go with me, for my mind is of non-cruelty."
Heroes who knew all dharmas, devoted to truth and the scriptures, intent on kshatriya dharma, wise, sacrificers who gave large fees...
